BUSINESS OWNER (Female, 58, $130K, Owner): #1 Chase / #2 Bank of America / #3 Bluevine / #4 U.S. Bank / #5 Wells Fargo. DIGITAL MARKETING FREELANCER (Male, 26, $65K, Freelancer): #1 Bluevine / #2 Lili / #3 Novo / #4 Chase / #5 Found. ELECTRICIAN (Male, 42, $90K, Electrician): #1 Capital One / #2 Chase / #3 Ally / #4 Bank of America / #5 Discover. SOFTWARE ENGINEER (Female, 29, $150K, Engineer): #1 Ally / #2 SoFi / #3 Chase / #4 Quontic / #5 Juno. Source: Profound AI Search Intelligence Platform · 762K+ brand mentions · Mar 2025 – Feb 2026 · Consistent across ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and Google AI Overviews.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2F9ccd50cq_IMG_2641.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

The banking-recommendations slide is the most concrete proof in the talk — **the same prompt produces 4 entirely different top-5 lists** across personas. *Chase* is a top-2 result for the business owner; **#4 for the freelancer**; #2 for the electrician; **#3 for the software engineer**. *Bluevine* is #3 for the business owner and **#1 for the freelancer**. The persona dimension is no longer a "nice to have" segmentation play — it's the *organizing variable* of the SERP.

- **Finding 1:** dramatically different brands surfaced per persona, persistently across the full 12 months
- **Finding 2:** significant volatility within each persona over time. Brands moved in and out of the recommendation set — you cannot let it stagnate
- **Finding 3:** citations differ by persona. **Reddit citations showed up for female business owners and female software engineers but NOT for the other personas tested.** Citation segmentation matters as much as brand selection
- **Finding 4:** AI infers economic stereotypes. Higher-end brands (Breville, Jura) recommended for software engineer and business owner personas. Lower-end brands (Keurig) for digital freelancer and electrician personas
- **Finding 5:** only Google Gemini explicitly factored salary. Job title alone was enough for the others to make the inference

### Experiment 2 — three Gmail accounts, controlled seeding

![Slide — "Enter DATA ANALYSIS. Patrick Schofield, Lead Relevance Engineer, iPullRank." Patrick rendered as a comic-book superhero in Times-Square-3D-grid space, with the AI SLOP enamel pin in the corner. The credit shoutout for the Experiment-2 dataset assembly.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fk39mt7gf_IMG_2640.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

- **Account A:** brand-new Gmail, no data, **baseline control**
- **Account B:** brand-new Gmail, opted into Personal Intelligence, but no seeded data
- **Account C:** Garrett's real personal Gmail with years of newsletters, receipts, photos, family content
- Then **seeded Account B** with: synthetic personal emails (*"hey Karen, ratio is a great coffee maker"*), photos taken in stores, brand-mentioning newsletters
- Ran the same 6 prompts across 8 products in all three accounts twice daily for several weeks

#### Experiment 2 results — the headline numbers

- **80% share of voice lift** for brands that were referenced in seeded personal emails
- Brands that did NOT show up in baseline (bottom 10–12 of the recommendation pool) suddenly **appeared 60% of the time** after email seeding
- Email seeding produced consistent lifts across every category tested
- Photos worked too, but mainly for physical products like coffee machines. Less effective for service categories
- Effect was strong enough across **500+ test runs** to be statistically meaningful within the dataset

### The wild specific examples

- **Direct mail showed up.** A local shoe service sent a postcard. Garrett's USPS mail-scanning service emailed him a photo of it. Personal Intelligence pulled that into AI Mode results, **citing "Potomac River Running" by name**
- **Unopened newsletters showed up.** Marc Giordano's newsletter mentioned a sponsor (Wakai) months ago. Garrett never opened the email. **It still surfaced in his AI Mode results** as a productivity recommendation
- **Spam emails showed up.** A spam email about a Costco award showed up in AI Mode personalization. (Garrett: *"do not take this as a green light to spam people"*)
- **Transactional emails dominate early.** Most personalization on his real account was driven by receipts and confirmation emails. AI Mode literally said *"you bought a metric ton of hoodies"* and recommended brands accordingly
- **Family member names leaked into recommendations.** AI Mode said *"for you and Jenny"* (his wife's name) and *"for Sammy"* (his daughter) when recommending streaming services

### The "it's not just SEO" through-line

- **Email marketing influences AI Mode.** How many SEOs are coordinating with their email team to win in AI?
- **Direct mail influences AI Mode.** How many SEOs are coordinating with their direct mail team?
- **Photos and social uploads influence AI Mode.** How many SEOs are coordinating with social and content?
- **Newsletter sponsorships and PR placements influence AI Mode** through content the user has even tangentially encountered
- The cross-functional collaboration message from Bianca's earlier session is now **mandatory, not optional**. AI personalization makes EVERY marketing channel a search input

### The search twin playbook

- Define your **priority personas** using audience data, not your imagination
- For each persona, **create a synthetic Gmail account.** Free, takes minutes
- **Opt that synthetic account into Personal Intelligence**
- **Seed the account like a real customer would behave:** subscribe to relevant newsletters, follow creators, listen to relevant podcasts, run expected searches, send the account your own marketing emails, simulate purchase confirmations
- Run priority prompts across the synthetic accounts on a **recurring schedule**
- Track how your brand and your competitors surface differently per persona over time

#### Industry-specific persona weighting

- **B2B / SaaS:** weight *jobs-to-be-done* heaviest in your synthetic account seeding
- **E-commerce / travel:** weight *psychographics and demographics*
- **Healthcare / personal finance:** *hybrid* of both
- **Don't seed everything.** Seed what matters for your industry and your audience

### Tools mentioned

- **SparkToro** (Rand Fishkin, Amanda Natividad) for audience research. Garrett ran SEO Week's opted-in attendee list through it to surface affinities, websites, apps, and topics
- **Similarweb** for AI Mode adoption and traffic data
- **Profound AI Search Intelligence Platform** — source for the 762K+ brand-mentions dataset behind the banking persona slide
- **Kevin Indig's research** on whether users actually choose AI-recommended brands. Finding: yes, top 3–5 from AI recommendations *are* influencing purchase behavior

### Personal Intelligence limitations to optimize around

- It does not understand **relationships**. If your spouse searches for something, it does not transfer to your context
- It misses **cross-device behavior**
- It misses **life changes** that are not explicitly mentioned in your accounts
- It misses **nuance** you do not state directly
- Garrett's view: these limits will improve marginally but never go away. **Plan for personalization noise as a permanent feature**

### Quotes worth keeping

> "It's not just SEO." — Garrett Sussman *(repeated as a refrain throughout the entire talk)*

> "Inboxes aren't a ranking signal, but the inbox matters." — Garrett Sussman

> "Brand influence shows up before the search." — Garrett Sussman

> "This is only the beginning." — Garrett Sussman

> "Personalization is the technical foundation for the future of more personalized AI agents, and a step on our journey towards AGI." — Google Personal Intelligence PDF (quoted)

> "Hopefully it works for us and we don't work for it." — Garrett Sussman

### My take

This is the **single most actionable talk of the conference so far**, and it's quietly the most important. Days 1–2 have been a slow build toward an inconvenient truth: **the search system is no longer querying a public web, it's querying *you***. Garrett gave us the proof, the methodology, and the playbook in 30 minutes.

The **banking persona slide** alone is going on every client deck I write for the next two quarters. *Chase* the #1 brand for an older female business owner, the *#4* brand for a 26-year-old male freelancer, the #2 brand for an electrician — same prompt, same model, four different SERPs. There is no "rank #1 for personal banking" anymore; there's only *"rank #1 for [persona]"* and you have to design and measure for that distinction.

The **80% share-of-voice lift from email seeding** is the line everyone will remember. Combined with Bianca Anderson's *"only 2 of 7 AEO functions"* framing from earlier this morning, the implication is unmistakable: **email, direct mail, social, PR, and even transactional confirmations are now ranking signals.** The cross-functional play is no longer a nice-to-have; it's the actual job.

The **search twin playbook** is the cleanest operational takeaway. I'm setting up 5 synthetic Gmails this week, one per priority persona, opting them all into Personal Intelligence, and starting a 90-day seeding-and-prompting protocol. The cost is zero. The intelligence value is enormous.

Pair this with Scott Stouffer's *"distinct centroid"* (Day 1) and Wil Reynolds's *"seen, believed, chosen"* (Day 2 morning) and Bianca Anderson's *"influence the other 5"* (Day 2 morning) and you have a coherent operating model: **build a distinct centroid → win the believability layer → coordinate cross-functionally to seed every personalization signal you can ethically influence → measure with synthetic search twins.**

The Apple Intelligence prediction is the wildcard. If Garrett's right about Google I/O in May (and the "third time's the charm" Apple ramp), this gets *much* more interesting *much* faster than most teams are planning for. Building search-twin infrastructure now is the cheapest insurance policy on the conference floor.

### Open questions

- [ ] How many synthetic search twins is the right number for a brand serving multiple personas?
- [ ] What is the right cadence for re-running prompts on synthetic accounts before drift sets in?
- [ ] How do you ethically seed synthetic accounts without crossing into spam territory or violating Gmail TOS?
- [ ] Will Apple Intelligence personalization use a fundamentally different model than Google Personal Intelligence, or will the same playbook work?
- [ ] Can you measure cross-channel attribution for AI Mode personalization (direct mail → AI citation, for example), or is this permanently dark?
- [ ] How will this evolve when LLMs negotiate with each other on behalf of users in agentic flows?

### Action items

- [ ] **Cross-functional outreach:** meet with email marketing, direct mail, PR, social to coordinate around AI Mode personalization
- [ ] **Audit transactional and post-purchase emails** your brand sends. Those are now AI Mode signals, not just CRM artifacts
- [ ] For B2B brands: prioritize **jobs-to-be-done** content seeded into synthetic personas. For e-commerce: prioritize **psychographic** content

## Amanda Milligan — Trifecta Content: Pages That Drive Rankings, Visibility & Engagement

**Key thesis:** *"Create high-quality content"* was always vague advice. Now it's **table stakes**. Quality is no longer the exception, it's the bare minimum. The stress is real: **Google wants 15,000 things, LLMs want every sentence to be a discrete extractable thought, YouTube wants 30 seconds, TikTok wants 3**. Amanda set out to find content that wins everywhere at once — ranks top-3 in Google, gets cited in AI, performs in email, gets shared on social. She had to dig hard. Real examples: **Angi's pricing guides** (proprietary cost data), **King Arthur Baking's ingredient weight chart** (fundamental reference data), and **Painting Chocolate's watercolor video tutorials** (visual expertise AI can't reproduce). The three creation triggers: do you own a **dataset** that makes sense for your brand to own? Do you have a **complicated-but-common problem** your audience has? Is there a **novel approach** you can coin and share?

![Amanda Milligan's trifecta test qualifications: top-3 Google rankings for keywords with real volume, citations in LLM answers for relevant queries, and engagement via email or social channels](/conference/seo-week-2026/amanda-milligan-1.jpg)

### TL;DR

"Create quality content" was always lazy advice and is now worthless — anyone can hit the old quality bar in 10 seconds with AI. The new bar is **trifecta content**: ranks top-3 in Google + cited in LLMs + above-average performer on email or social, all in one piece. Real examples are rare but real: Angi's proprietary pricing guides, King Arthur's ingredient weight chart (so useful bakers call it their *"Bible"* on Reddit), Painting Chocolate's watercolor tutorials AI literally can't reproduce. The three creation triggers: **own a dataset**, **answer a complicated-but-common problem** (ideally visual), or **coin a novel approach** (Klaviyo's *"loot marketing,"* Amanda Natividad's *"zero-click marketing"*). Pick one, commit, stop trying to please all four gatekeepers by default.

### "Create high-quality content" was always lazy advice

- Amanda has been giving and receiving this advice for 15 years. She estimates she's said it personally **at least 4.5 billion times**
- The Regina George frame: *"How many of you have been personally victimized by me telling you to create great content?"*
- The advice has always been *"if you see it, you know it."* **That doesn't fly anymore**
- Anyone can create content that meets the old quality bar in **10 seconds with AI** now. The bar moved overnight

### A short history of "quality content"

- **Penguin and Panda era (early 2010s):** *"quality"* meant any non-spam content. Easy to win, low bar. Amanda came up in this era as a journalism student who didn't want to be a reporter
- **Skyscraper era (mid 2010s):** see what's ranking, do something better. UX, graphics, missing angles. Quality was **visible improvement**
- **E-E-A-T (2022):** the addition of **Experience** to E-A-T. Suddenly the writer had to have actually done the thing, or interview someone who had. **Quality became harder to manufacture**
- **Search Everywhere (now):** Google was the only gatekeeper for a decade. Now TikTok, YouTube, LLMs, Reddit, and every AI assistant are all gatekeepers with **different rules**

### The four-gatekeeper stress test

![The four gatekeepers' competing demands: Google's endless checklist, LLMs wanting standalone sentences, YouTube's 30-second hook, and TikTok demanding three seconds](/conference/seo-week-2026/amanda-milligan-2.jpg)

- **Google:** here are 15,000 things you need to do
- **LLMs:** is every sentence a complete discrete thought, you idiot?
- **YouTube:** if you don't get my attention in 30 seconds, you may as well not exist
- **TikTok:** hold my beer, do it in three
- Hitting all four with one piece of content sounds impossible. But the alternative (creating four versions of everything) **doesn't scale**

### The pivot — trifecta content

- **Old advice (Amanda's included):** one piece of content, one primary goal. Don't dilute the focus
- **New reality:** if quality is the baseline, you need to extract more value per piece. **Make it work across multiple gatekeepers without becoming generic**
- **Trifecta content** = ranks top-3 in Google + cited or mentioned in LLMs + above-average performer on email or social
- Amanda spent embarrassing hours hunting for examples. Asked every SEO Slack she's in. **One person responded**
- The content does exist. It's just **rare and intentional**

### What is NOT typically trifecta content

- **State-of-X reports:** do well on social and PR, rarely searched in Google
- **Event content:** tied to a moment, doesn't compound
- **Trend content:** works for big brands with brand search demand, less for smaller brands
- **Don't stop creating these.** Just don't expect them to do all four jobs. Apply the old goal-specific framing to them

### Example 1 — Angi's pricing guides

- **Caroline Gilbert** (Angi, formerly Angie's List) was the one Slack response Amanda got
- Angi has **proprietary cost data from millions of contractor jobs** (HVAC, painting, plumbing, etc.). They built dozens of pricing-guide pages from that data
- Result: **ranking #1** for terms with hundreds to thousands of monthly searches
- Result: **outperformed every other email send** when distributed to their list
- Result: **most cited Angi pages in AI responses.** The brand is now *the answer* when AI is asked about home-improvement pricing
- **Why it works:** reference-worthy, actionable (helps decisions, not just entertainment), replicable as a **programmatic content set**

### Example 2 — King Arthur Baking's ingredient weight chart

![King Arthur Baking posts its Ingredient Weight Chart to its own subreddit, and bakers respond with glowing comments like "I visit this at least once per baking session"](/conference/seo-week-2026/amanda-milligan-3.jpg)

- The single most boring page on King Arthur's site: a conversion table for cups, grams, ounces of every common baking ingredient
- **#1 in Google** for nearly every variant of *"ingredient weight chart"* queries
- AI **specifically names** King Arthur's chart when recommending conversion resources, not just citing them
- **Most cited page on the entire King Arthur site**
- The wild part: King Arthur posts the chart to its own subreddit. Bakers comment *"this is my Bible," "I use this every day."* **Reddit, glowing comments, on a static reference table**
- **Why it works:** practical, actionable, fundamental to using their actual products (flour). The brand association is what beats AI's tendency to just answer the question itself
- This is the cleanest example of *"data that has to be authoritative because YOU are the authority"*

### Example 3 — Painting Chocolate (visual tutorials)

- For brands without proprietary data or massive name recognition, **video is the shortcut**
- **Painting Chocolate** is a small watercolor education site. One YouTube tutorial got **20,000+ views**
- The same content shared to Instagram performed strongly
- Same content **ranks high in Google** for the watercolor tutorial query
- Cited in AI Mode for the same query
- **Why it works:** AI is genuinely **worse than humans at producing visual tutorials**. Step-by-step painting instruction can't be summarized into 10 bullet points. First-person experience is required (E-E-A-T applies)
- The lane is open right now. AI catching up is a question of time. **Use the window**

### Bonus — Klaviyo's "Loot Marketing"

- Klaviyo **invented and pushed a new term**: *"loot marketing"*
- 50K+ views on YouTube, strong Instagram performance
- Doesn't fully meet the trifecta criteria yet because almost nobody searches *"loot marketing"* in Google (~100–200 monthly searches)
- But: **when you coin a category, you own it.** Search demand grows. You're the only authority for the duration of the build
- The lesson: **innovation is still rewarded.** Coining a phrase is a slow-burn trifecta play if the underlying concept is real

### The three creation triggers (you only need one)

![The three questions behind trifecta content: what dataset should your brand own, what complicated-but-common problem can you answer, and what novel concept can you coin](/conference/seo-week-2026/amanda-milligan-4.jpg)

- **Trigger 1 — Do you own a dataset it makes sense for your brand to own?** Zillow owns housing. AAA owns gas prices. Strava owns running pace data. Angi owns home-improvement costs. King Arthur owns baking conversions. **What's yours?**
- **Trigger 2 — What's a complicated-but-common problem your audience has that you can answer?** Especially if it's **visual**. *"How to pack for two weeks in a carry-on"* is text-summarizable. *"How to bind a quilt"* is not. Find your version
- **Trigger 3 — Is there a novel approach, process, or philosophy you can coin and share?** Amanda Natividad's *"zero-click marketing"* is a category-defining example. *"Quiet quitting."* **Categories you name, you own**
- **Pick one.** Don't try all three at once

### Why naming things matters (the trifecta phrase itself)

- Amanda kept getting stuck explaining *"content that ranks in Google AND gets cited in AI AND works in email AND drives social"* to people
- It was tiring. So she **named it**
- *"Trifecta content"* is faster, more memorable, **easier to evangelize**
- For your industry: what are you constantly explaining over and over? **That's a candidate for a coined phrase you can own**

### Quotes worth keeping

> "Quality content used to be the exception. Now it's the baseline."

> "You can't say it's quality if you can produce something that meets the same caliber in 10 seconds."

> "Google wants 15,000 things, LLMs want every sentence to be a discrete thought, YouTube wants 30 seconds, TikTok says hold my beer."

> "Reference-worthy, not link-worthy. The brand mention is the new link."

> "Data for data's sake doesn't compound. Data that helps people make decisions does."

> "Innovation is still rewarded, even if it doesn't fit the perfect criteria."

> "What are you constantly explaining over and over? That's where you should coin a phrase."

### Open questions

- For B2B SaaS without obvious proprietary data, what's the equivalent of the Angi pricing play?
- How long is the visual-tutorial window before AI's video understanding closes the gap?
- For brands without an existing audience to coin a term to, how do you bootstrap the *"loot marketing"* play?
- Is there a real risk of **trifecta dilution** where content tries to please everyone and ranks for nothing?
- How do you measure trifecta performance in a way that justifies the longer production cycles to leadership?
- What happens to trifecta content's distribution advantage if AI search adoption keeps eating into Google share?

### Action items

- Run the **trifecta test** on your top 20 pages: do they rank top-3 in Google AND get cited in AI AND perform on email or social? How many pass all three?
- Identify your **proprietary dataset.** What does your brand uniquely know? Look at internal data, customer behavior, transactional records
- For each dataset, design a **programmatic page set** (the Angi model). One template, many variants, all ownable
- Audit content for **visual-tutorial opportunities.** Find complicated-but-common problems your audience has where **seeing beats reading**
- Identify what you constantly explain over and over. **Coin the phrase.** Build the term that makes you the category creator
- Stop applying the old *"one goal per piece"* rule to high-investment content. **Layer goals deliberately. Don't dilute**
- For each existing top page, identify which of the three triggers it leans on. **Strengthen the lean.** Don't try to retrofit all three
- Pair the **King Arthur Reddit pattern** with your reference content. Post the data to your own community. Watch what happens
- For brands without name recognition, prioritize **video tutorials with first-person expertise.** Use the window before AI's visual capabilities close the gap
- Read **Amanda Natividad's** work on *zero-click marketing* for the precedent on how a coined phrase becomes a category
- Pair this with **John Doherty's** session: production capacity is not the constraint. **Strategy and concept are.** Trifecta content is a strategy framework, not a production pipeline
takeaways: 'Quality content' used to be the exception — now it's the baseline; anyone can hit the old bar in 10 seconds with AI
Four gatekeepers, one piece: Google, LLMs, YouTube, TikTok — trifecta content wins across all of them in a single asset
Angi's proprietary pricing guides rank #1, outperform email, and are the most-cited Angi pages in AI — proprietary data that makes sense for the brand to own
King Arthur's ingredient weight chart: #1 in Google, specifically named by AI, and called 'my Bible' on Reddit — practical reference data tied to actual products
Visual tutorials (Painting Chocolate watercolor YouTube) are the open lane — AI is genuinely worse at visual step-by-steps; use the window before it closes
Three creation triggers, pick ONE: own a dataset, answer a complicated-but-common (ideally visual) problem, or coin a novel category (Klaviyo's 'loot marketing', Natividad's 'zero-click marketing')
State-of-X reports, event content, and trend content are NOT trifecta content — don't stop making them, but don't expect them to do all four jobs
Name what you keep explaining — 'trifecta content' itself is the example: naming a pattern is a slow-burn trifecta play

## Wil Reynolds — Visibility Is Not Enough: Seen, Believed, Chosen

**Key thesis:** The whole industry has spent the day talking about visibility. Wil's argument: **visibility on its own is a vanity metric**. The job of marketing is to take someone from **seen → believed → chosen**. AI search is repeating the same mistake SEO made in 2006–2008 — ranking for everything and proving nothing. Most "AI visibility" tools measure **shots on goal, not goals scored**. If your prospects don't believe you exist on the topic, don't believe you're credible on it, or don't have a reason to choose you over a near-identical competitor, all the visibility in the world is wasted. **Stop being a McNugget maker pretending to be a Michelin star. Pick a side.**

![Wil Reynolds on stage in his red Wu-Tang shirt, opening Day 2 of SEO Week 2026 with the seen-believed-chosen keynote](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fcpz6zgk3_IMG_2620.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

### Personal note

Wil cares about other humans. He is transparent. He talks facts. He shares stats based on his own data. A genuinely great person and human and search expert who I respect.

He shared every tool, every resource, the full audio, transcript, and slide deck publicly — and asked for nothing in return except contributions to a homeless youth nonprofit he has supported for **15 years (Covenant House)**. He sleeps outside every November to raise money for it.

**Resources:** [info.seerinteractive.com/wil-reynolds-seo-week-2026](https://info.seerinteractive.com/wil-reynolds-seo-week-2026)

### TL;DR

The whole industry has spent the day talking about visibility. Wil's argument: visibility on its own is a vanity metric. The job of marketing is to take someone from **seen → believed → chosen**. AI search is repeating the same mistake SEO made in 2006–2008, ranking for everything and proving nothing. Most "AI visibility" tools measure **shots on goal, not goals scored**. If your prospects don't believe you exist on the topic, don't believe you're credible on it, or don't have a reason to choose you over a near-identical competitor, all the visibility in the world is wasted. **Stop being a McNugget maker pretending to be a Michelin star. Pick a side.**

### The core framework — Seen, Believed, Chosen

- **Seen** — showing up in AI answers, search results, social. Visibility
- **Believed** — the prospect develops a belief about your brand. Followers, newsletter signups, brand search, branded prompt usage
- **Chosen** — they part with their money. Pipeline, leads, closed deals, revenue
- Most "AI visibility" tracking only measures the first one. The whole industry is celebrating face-offs while no one is putting the puck in the net
- **Michelin example:** drove every road in France to find great restaurants. The star *became a belief*. Booking a starred restaurant has a 6-month wait. Seen, believed, chosen — executed at the highest level
- **Ramp counter-example:** built a believable brand through quality content and CEO appearances, then ran *"Top Restaurants in Minnesota"* zombie content and 5× sequence emails that turned a prospect (Wil's CFO) off. All the goodwill burned for a vanity output

#### SEO Math vs. GEO Math

![SEO Math vs. GEO Math (Wil Reynolds, SEO Week 2026 by iPullRank/airops). Top-left: SEO Math — Keyword MSV → If I can get you Ranked → MSV × CTR = Visits → Visits × CVR = Conv's → Conv × Value = ROI! Bottom-right: GEO Math — Search volume (no idea), Personalization (no idea), CTR (no idea), Visits (1/20th of SEO), Conversions from AI (low). The point: every input on the GEO side is unknown or de minimis, yet the industry is selling it like SEO Math.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2F0mrtad1m_IMG_2621.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

- **SEO Math** is a clean chain you could brief a CFO on: Keyword MSV → CTR → Visits → CVR → Conv → Value → ROI. Every input has a known data source
- **GEO Math** has every input marked *"no idea"* — search volume unknown, personalization opaque, CTR unmeasurable, visits roughly 1/20th of SEO, conversions from AI low
- *"If you can't define the math, you can't promise the outcome. Stop pretending GEO is a performance channel — it's not, yet"*

### The "this or that" choice

- Are you a **strategist** or a **loophole-ist**?
- Are you trying to make your company an authority in their domain, or are you chasing **domain authority** via tactics that won't survive the next algorithm shift?
- Two real brands selling **ethical jeans**: one ranks 5, one ranks 55 in Google. The 55 brand is the one that actually flies to factories, repairs jeans for life, works with scientists on water-impact dyes. **In ChatGPT, the 5 brand has zero AI visibility.** Visibility built on tactics evaporates when the surface changes
- Pick a side, but recognize that loophole strategies have a half-life — and the half-life is now measured in **months, not years**

### Reddit as the believability gut-check

- **Tactic:** when a tool or vendor produces a "best of" list and your brand is in the top 3, scrape every relevant Reddit thread for the same query
- Pull every brand mentioned by real humans across those threads
- If your brand has zero mentions and competitors are mentioned 50+ times, **the listicle is fiction**. The humans have already voted
- Use the Reddit signal as the **believability filter** on AI visibility wins. *Visible without believed = dead on arrival*
- **Sales script:** *"I see your visibility is up. Here are the brands real humans actually mention for this problem. You are not on it. Are we trying to be visible, or are we trying to make money?"*

### Watch real humans do real tasks

- Seer interviewed **30 real people** doing real tasks in ChatGPT and Gemini, captured **114 prompts**
- **Cost: about $800 through Outset** (AI moderates the user interviews)
- **Findings:** prompts ranged from **4 words to 119 words** for the same task. Most "fan-out" research tools are dressed-up People Also Ask. They are *not* reflective of how real humans interact
- **50%+ of human prompts include brands the user already knows.** The implication: **branded prompt accuracy is the first job.** Owning your own narrative comes before chasing non-branded queries
- Watch how often AI proactively offers next steps after the answer (*"I can also do this for you"*). That **post-answer surface is the new conversion moment**, and almost no one is tracking it
- Replace *"scale everything, look at the numbers"* research culture with **watching 30 humans do the task**

### The brand-prompt audit (start here, not at non-branded)

- Most agencies want to start by ranking for non-branded queries. **Wrong order**
- Start with: *when someone prompts your brand name, what does the AI say?* Is it accurate, on-brand, and aligned with your positioning?
- **Define your brand mission and what you actually do (and what you don't do)** before measuring
- For each branded prompt, score whether AI corroborates or contradicts the positioning
- If AI says you are slow, your account manager turnover is high, your firm is "too tinkery" — those are public narratives competitors are exploiting
- The next layer: pull all sales call transcripts, run them against your prompts, find where AI is missing context that real prospects already discuss with your sales team
- **Tool Wil built:** a brand-prompt comparison tool that takes "your brand vs. competitor" prompts, pulls answers across training data and live web, gives you a spider chart of strengths and weaknesses

### The visibility + believability dashboard

- Stop letting visibility tools sell you a flat line of citations as success
- Overlay visibility metrics with **believability metrics**: branded search trend, newsletter signups, direct traffic, social traffic, referral traffic, form fills — and finally pipeline
- If visibility is up and signups are flat, branded search is flat, pipeline is flat, **you are running a vanity program**. Confront it
- **Trust channels (direct, social, referral)** are harder to track but convert at **1.5× to 5×** the rate of organic for Seer's own data
- *"Show me your GA"* is the new ante. If an agency cannot or will not show downstream traffic and pipeline impact, the visibility number means nothing

### The Seer turnover counter-attack (case study)

- A competitor's prompt set leaked. Wil's team ran deep research with their own brand inserted: *"given X criteria, who would you pick?"*
- AI surfaced a negative claim: *"Seer has high account manager turnover"* (sourced from one bad review out of an entire 20+ year history)
- **Showed up in 38% of branded prompts.** Material. Whether true or false — fixable
- **Step 1:** published internal client shout-outs publicly with real client quotes
- **Step 2:** published Seer's actual employee retention data, then benchmarked it against agency averages from deep research. Found their numbers are above average
- **Step 3:** built content explicitly addressing the false narrative with sourced data
- **Result:** the negative claim disappeared from branded prompts for a stretch, came back, now iterating on a second wave of brand-defense content
- **Generalizable framework:** AI defaults to "balanced" answers. *It will dig to result 150 to find a con.* The fix is publishing your own pros and cons backed by data so AI cites you, not third-party complaints

### The McNugget vs. Michelin frame

- Both McDonald's chicken nuggets and a Michelin chicken dish are technically chicken
- McDonald's knows what it makes is fast, predictable, and disposable. **There is no McNugget executive asking "have we earned a Michelin star yet?"**
- The SEO industry is full of people pretending to be Michelin while shipping McNugget content at scale
- **Decide which one you are.** Both can run a business. **Mixing the two breaks the brand**

### Quotes worth keeping

> "The job of marketing was never to be visible. It was to be seen, believed, and chosen." — Wil Reynolds

> "Visibility is just an opportunity. Shots on goal. The job is to take the puck to the net." — Wil Reynolds

> "You will never produce a thing anyone wants if you keep playing rack-and-roll marketing." — Wil Reynolds

> "Followers don't pay. Newsletter signups don't pay. Pipeline pays." — Wil Reynolds

> "You can have all the visibility in the world. If people don't believe or trust you, you don't get chosen." — Wil Reynolds

> "50% of the time, real humans put brands they already know in their prompts." — Wil Reynolds

> "AI defaults to balanced. It will dig to result 150 to find a con." — Wil Reynolds

> "Stop letting other people own the narrative about your brand because you won't." — Wil Reynolds

> "Open up GA. Show me. That's the new ante." — Wil Reynolds

### My take

After a full Day 1 of *measure-the-mechanism* talks (Mike King, Krishna, Jori, Metehan, Scott, Jeff), Wil walks on stage Day 2 in a Wu-Tang shirt and tells the entire room **the mechanism doesn't matter if no one believes you or chooses you.** It's the perfect contrast keynote — and the right one to open Day 2 ("The Psychology") on.

The **SEO Math vs. GEO Math** slide is the cleanest single visual I've seen for explaining to a CFO why "AI visibility" reporting is currently theater. SEO has every input quantified; GEO has *"no idea"* in every box. If you can't define the math, you can't promise the outcome. That single slide is going on the wall in our team room.

The **Reddit gut-check** tactic is the most operational thing I'm taking home. The next time someone shows me a "we ranked #2 in this AI listicle" win, the response is going to be: *"pull the matching Reddit threads — show me the human signal."* If the listicle disagrees with humans, the listicle is fiction.

The **Seer turnover case study** is the framework I needed for client work. AI hallucinates *"balanced"* answers — it will surface a 1-in-1000 negative review as *"a known concern."* The defense is publishing your own pros AND cons with sourced data, so the model cites you, not a complaint thread. That's a content brief I'm writing tomorrow.

Pair this keynote with Jeff Coyle's "passages have to win" + Scott Stouffer's "centroid is what AI calculates" from yesterday and the picture is complete: **the mechanism gets you in the candidate set, the believability gets you chosen.** Wil's the missing half of the equation.

The personal note matters too. He's giving away the entire deck, transcript, and toolset for a Covenant House donation. That's seen-believed-chosen executed in real time on the conference floor — and it's exactly why his believability metric is unfair to compete with.

### Open questions

- [ ] What is the right cost ceiling for running 30 real-human task interviews per major client engagement?
- [ ] How do you measure the *"post-answer surface"* (AI proactively offering next steps) at scale?
- [ ] What is the cleanest way to operationalize *"show me GA"* as the new agency-vetting standard across an industry that has built its margins on opacity?
- [ ] For B2C brands without a sales team, what replaces sales-call transcripts as a source of real-prospect language?
- [ ] How do you defend a brand from a single negative review getting amplified by AI's balanced-answer default at scale?

### Action items

- [ ] Run a **branded-prompt audit** before any non-branded GEO work. Score each branded answer for accuracy and on-brand alignment
- [ ] Use **Outset** (or equivalent) to interview 20–30 real users doing your priority tasks in ChatGPT and Gemini. Budget: **roughly $800**
- [ ] Pull all sales call transcripts, run them against priority prompts, find context the AI is missing that prospects already discuss
- [ ] **Reddit gut-check** every "best of" list your brand appears in. Compare against real human mentions. Kill the list if it doesn't match
- [ ] Build a **visibility + believability dashboard**. Add branded search, newsletter signups, direct traffic, social traffic, referral traffic, pipeline. Stop reporting visibility alone
- [ ] Identify negative narratives AI is repeating about your brand. Address each one with sourced, data-backed content from your own domain
- [ ] **Publish proprietary data** (employee retention, client retention, methodology stats) so AI cites your numbers instead of third-party speculation
- [ ] For agency vetting: **ask any prospective vendor to open their own GA before signing**. If they refuse, walk
- [ ] Stop publishing zombie content (best-of lists for places nobody actually drives across). Every piece needs a real human reason to exist
- [ ] Capture content from real subject-matter experts before editors strip the unique perspective out
- [ ] **Donate to Covenant House.** Wil sleeps outside every November for them — the least we can do for a free deck like this

### People to follow up

- **Wil Reynolds** — Founder & CEO, Seer Interactive · [linkedin.com/in/wilreynolds](https://www.linkedin.com/in/wilreynolds/) · Full deck, transcript, audio, and toolset: [info.seerinteractive.com/wil-reynolds-seo-week-2026](https://info.seerinteractive.com/wil-reynolds-seo-week-2026) · Donate to Covenant House.
takeaways: The job of marketing is seen → believed → chosen, not visibility alone
GEO Math has 'no idea' in every box (search volume, CTR, personalization). If you can't define the math, don't promise the outcome
Use Reddit as the believability gut-check on any 'best-of' AI listicle — kill it if humans haven't voted for you
Watch 30 real humans do real tasks (Outset, ~$800) instead of scaling fake prompt sets
Start with a branded-prompt audit before chasing non-branded queries — 50%+ of human prompts include known brands
AI defaults to 'balanced' answers and digs to result 150 to find a con — defend with your own sourced pros and cons
Stop being a McNugget maker pretending to be a Michelin star. Pick a side

## Bianca Anderson — SEOs Own Less Than We Think: Three Plays for Cross-Functional Influence

**Key thesis:** SEOs only own **2 of 7 AEO functions** on the typical org chart, and **90% of citations come from third-party sources** we do not control. The skill that matters now is **influence, not ownership**. Bianca shares three plays for working across teams who hold the levers we need: **constraints first** (treat blockers like collaborators), **make it theirs** (give up the starting point to unlock investment), and **SEO as a service** (build something that solves a shared pain so the relationship has a reason to exist). The Japanese honeybee uses precision collaboration to kill a hornet ten times its size. **SEOs can do the same.**

![Bianca Anderson on stage at SEO Week 2026, opening her cross-functional-influence talk in the pink top + jeans](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fvu3ahyd3_IMG_2622%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

### TL;DR

SEOs only own 2 of 7 AEO functions on the typical org chart, and 90% of citations come from third-party sources we do not control. The skill that matters now is influence, not ownership. Three plays: constraints first (treat blockers like collaborators), make it theirs (give up the starting point to unlock investment), SEO as a service (build something that solves a shared pain so the relationship has a reason to exist). The Japanese honeybee analogy: 12mm bees beat 2-inch hornets through precision collaboration. SEOs can do the same.

### The Japanese honeybee analogy

- The Japanese honeybee (*Apis cerana japonica*) is **12mm long**. Its enemy, the Asian giant hornet, is up to **2 inches with a 3-inch wingspan**. A single hornet can kill **40 honeybees per minute**
- The bees' defense: they let a scout hornet enter the hive, then **500 bees swarm it, vibrate their flight muscles, and raise the ball to exactly 47°C**. The hornet dies. The bees survive
- **The precision matters.** 46°C, the hornet survives. 48°C, the bees die too. The window is **one degree**
- The metaphor: SEOs cannot beat AI visibility challenges alone. We need precise, coordinated collaboration with teams we do not directly control

### The influence gap

- Per **Eli Schwartz's framework**: SEO owns only **2 of 7 AEO media functions** (technical schema, model visibility/auditing)
- The other 5 (informed presence, content depth, narrative, entity definition, etc.) sit with **brand, PR, product marketing, and legal** teams
- Compounding the issue: **90% of AI citations come from third-party** reviews, forums, press, and community content built by other teams
- SEOs are uniquely primed to lead AI visibility but are at the mercy of teams we do not control. **That is the influence gap**

### Play 1 — Constraints First (the legal-team story)

**Definition:** center the concerns of blocking teams *before* you build anything, so the finished product reflects what will actually ship.

- **Setting:** ~50 keywords for competitive comparison content at Hims and Hers, all lower-funnel and high-revenue. Editorial said *"we tried that, legal killed it"*
- **The standard pattern that fails:** build the strategy → build the content → send to legal for approval → legal says no
- **The flipped pattern that worked:** go to legal FIRST and ask *"what are you worried about?"* Treat their fears as the **input to the brief**, not the blocker at the end
- Legal said: *"what if competitors retaliate?"* → translated to brief constraint: only use verifiable public facts, no speculation
- Legal said: *"you cannot say we are best or that we outperform anyone"* → translated to: use neutral language. *"Different"* not *"better."* *"Hims has providers, X is a marketplace"* not *"Hims is superior"*
- Legal said: *"this content type can read aggressive"* → translated to: acknowledge competitor strengths earnestly. *"Both options are legitimate. Here are the differences. You decide"*

#### Result: Legal said yes. 50 pages, 7 figures of attributed revenue.

![Bianca's "Legal said yes." slide — orange honeycomb backdrop with bee mascots and a "Bee mine or Buzz off" Polaroid. The headline marks the moment a project that had been blocked for years finally cleared legal because the constraints were the input to the brief, not the blocker at the end.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fdg2efkcl_IMG_2624%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

#### Two questions before applying constraints first

1. **Is the fear addressable?** Can you actually solve for it in the brief?
2. **Will the final output still be worth making?** Will the constrained version still drive results?

If yes to both: build inside the constraints.
If no to either: **don't build.** The constraints will make the work worthless.

**Bonus benefit:** building inside legal's constraints kept Hims out of the self-promotional listicle trap. Per *Search Engine Land* (Feb 2025), some SaaS brands saw **30–50% visibility drops** after publishing self-ranked "best" pages. Google is cracking down on that pattern.

#### What the published page actually looked like

![Hims's "Hims vs. Keeps for Hair Loss 2025: How Do They Compare?" comparison page — clean editorial layout, doctor-reviewed byline (Reviewed by Mike Bohl, MD · Written by Grace Gallagher), TOC sidebar (Getting Started, Getting a Prescription, Products, Bundle Options, etc.), and neutral-language framing throughout. The page that legal "would never approve" — until the constraints became the brief.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fz7yrbi3r_IMG_2625%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

The doctor-reviewed byline (*Reviewed by Mike Bohl, MD · Written by Grace Gallagher*) is doing two jobs: legal cover (a credentialed reviewer materially weakens any "misleading marketing" claim) **and** E-E-A-T fuel (verifiable expertise signal AI can corroborate). That dual-purpose pattern is the unlock — the constraint *became* the optimization.

### Play 2 — Make It Theirs (the Erica Garza story)

**Definition:** hand over the starting point to the people whose investment makes the work worth making. Different from constraints first — that's about navigating blockers; this is about generating *genuine investment* from collaborators.

#### The HubSpot E-E-A-T Playbook (from Bianca's prior life)

![HubSpot E-E-A-T SEO Playbook for Search Generative Experience — internal document authored by Bianca Anderson (EN Blog SEO Lead, HubSpot, 2023). 8 chapters: 01 Productive Perspectives for Content Creation (highlighted/circled), 02 Original Insights & Data Repository, 03 Scale Primary Research Capabilities, 04 Map Authors to Topic Clusters, 05 Content Freshness Optimization at Scale, 06 SGE Monitoring & Performance Tracking, 07 About Us Pages Expansion, 08 HubSpot-ified E-E-A-T Checklist.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2F9dh1lmgd_IMG_2626%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

The playbook reads like a comprehensive AEO blueprint. Chapter 01 — **Productive Perspectives** — is the seed for the Erica Garza story: first-person writing, real product demos, controversial stances, original research. Notice that Original Insights & Data Repository (Chapter 2) is the seed for Play 3 below.

#### The Erica Garza unlock

- **Context:** Bianca built the E-E-A-T playbook at HubSpot, including *"productive perspectives"* (first-person writing, real product demos, controversial stances, original research)
- **Setting:** Erica Garza, MFA from Columbia, published in *Time*, *Glamour*, *The Cut*. A Hims and Hers staff writer being handed briefs and told to write
- **The unlock:** stop giving writers briefs and keywords. **Let them pitch freely.** Their voice, their vision, their byline. End-to-end ownership
- Brand and editorial pushback addressed by **reverse engineering**: writers pitch topics first, *then* SEO finds best-fit keywords with form/forum signals in the SERP, *then* validates product fit
- **Results:** content **out-ranked Reddit** ("too afraid to ask" threads), **converted 2× internal blog benchmarks**, scaled to before-and-after and doctor-led review formats
- **The deeper win:** Erica got an Instagram DM from a reader: *"thank you for giving me hope."* That cannot be manufactured by mandate
- **The principle:** *"You cannot mandate humanity into existence with content marketing. You can only create the conditions for it to happen."*

### Play 3 — SEO as a Service (the shared source repository)

**Definition:** build something that solves shared pain as a way to open the relationship, establish trust, and create a reason to keep working together.

- **Setting:** Bianca had no relationship with the internal community team. Three teams (organic, editorial, community) were separately hunting for the same data: clinician quotes, proprietary insights, customer voices

#### The Shared Source Repository

![The "Shared Source Repository" diagram — central node (Shared Source Repository) connected to 4 inputs: Clinician Quotes, Proprietary Data, Community Insights, External Experts. Bianca-as-bee mascot in the center with a flower. The tactical visualization of "build something that solves shared pain so the relationship has a reason to exist."](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fghioi3hq_IMG_2627%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

- **Solution:** a simple **Google Sheet**. Cleanly mapped to outline/title format. Bianca seeded it with clinician quotes from various sources. Community added customer testimonials. Editorial added external expert interview contacts
- The repository **took on a life of its own**. Pictures, video, survey data started getting added without prompting
- **The real win was not the repository.** It was the meetings to discuss it, where Bianca could plant other ideas. The relationship had a reason to exist

#### When SEO as a service fails (the shared media library)

- Bianca tried the same play with a shared media library across paid, social, community. **It failed**
- **Why:** editorial had massive backlog (genuine pain). Social, community, and paid had perfectly fine processes already (no shared pain)
- **The pain has to be genuinely shared.** You cannot solve YOUR problem and call it shared
- **The spectrum:**
  - **Extracting** from the relationship (asking for favors) →
  - **Being useful sometimes** (responding to requests) →
  - **SEO as a service** (building durable infrastructure that runs without you)
- *"The hardest team to get into is often the one where nobody knows they need you. The SEO as a service play opens the door through genuine usefulness, not persuasion"*

### The big synthesis

- **Constraints first** → builds **credibility** (you listened, you adapted)
- **Make it theirs** → builds **investment** (collaborators care about the outcome, not just the deliverable)
- **SEO as a service** → builds **dependency** (the org cannot run without you)
- Together: **you stop optimizing what you own and start influencing what you do not**
- *"SEOs sometimes get a bad rap because cross-functional teams misunderstand what we are trying to do. SEO is the legal of marketing. Just trying to make Google happy. We know that is not true. Others don't always."* — Bianca Dininno Friedman, quoted

### Quotes worth keeping

> "It is not the strongest that survives, but the most adaptable." — Darwin (applied to legal pushback)

> "Influence gets you a yes. Investment gives you a partner." — Bianca Anderson

> "You cannot mandate humanity into existence with content marketing. You can only create the conditions for it to happen." — Bianca Anderson

> "The pain has to be genuinely shared, and you have to actually solve it." — Bianca Anderson

> "If we stop focusing on just optimizing what we own and start focusing on influencing what we don't, we can influence way more than we think." — Bianca Anderson

> "You only own 2 of 7 AEO functions. Influence the other 5." — Bianca Anderson

### My take

After Wil Reynolds opened Day 2 with the *seen-believed-chosen* reframe (the *what*), Bianca delivers the *how do I get my org to actually do this?* answer. This is the most operational talk of the conference so far — every play has a real-world before/after with a number attached.

The **Eli Schwartz "2 of 7"** stat is the line I'm taking back to my team. We have spent the last 18 months arguing internally about whether AEO is "our" surface or "marketing's" surface. The honest answer is: it's **everyone's**, and SEO owns the smallest piece. The job isn't to claim more territory — it's to **become indispensable to the people who own the rest**. That's a different career skill than the one most SEOs trained for.

**Constraints-first** is the play I want to ship by next week. We have at least three projects parked because someone (legal, brand, compliance) said no after the work was done. Going to those teams *first* with a question (not a deck) is a 30-minute meeting that probably unlocks 7 figures.

**Make it theirs** is the harder one because it requires giving up control. But the Erica Garza outcome (out-ranked Reddit + 2× conversion + a reader DM saying "thank you for giving me hope") is the proof that the *unlock* is bigger than the *control*. The reader-DM moment is also exactly the kind of *memory* moment Ross Simmonds will keynote Day 3 about — emotional, repeatable, branded.

**SEO as a service** is the long game. The shared-source-repository diagram is going to be the wallpaper of my next quarter. The failure case (shared media library) is just as instructive — *the pain has to be genuinely shared*. Most "shared infrastructure" projects fail because one team made up the pain on behalf of the other four.

Pair this with Jori Ford's HEO scorecard (Day 1) and Scott Stouffer's centroid framework: **Jori tells you what to measure, Scott tells you the position to hold, Bianca tells you how to actually get the org to move.** That's the trifecta.

### Open questions

- [ ] How do you scale **constraints first** when the blocker is a centralized legal or compliance team serving 50+ marketing teams?
- [ ] What's the right governance structure for **make it theirs** when a writer's byline becomes a load-bearing E-E-A-T signal and the writer leaves the company?
- [ ] How do you measure the ROI of **SEO as a service** infrastructure investments to leadership when the value is relationship capital, not direct attribution?
- [ ] For agency-side SEOs without internal-team access, how does this framework adapt? Are there client-side analogs to legal, brand, editorial, and community?
- [ ] How does this play change when the cross-functional teams in question are themselves being squeezed by AI (writers, brand, PR)?

### Action items

- [ ] **Map your org against Eli Schwartz's 7 AEO functions.** Mark which 2 you own and which 5 you do not
- [ ] For each function you do not own, identify the team lead. Build a relationship plan for each
- [ ] Identify one project currently blocked by legal, brand, or compliance. Run the **constraints-first play**: ask the blocker what they're worried about FIRST, before building anything
- [ ] Translate each fear into an actionable brief constraint. Apply both questions: **is it addressable, and will the output still be worth making?**
- [ ] Identify one talented internal contributor whose creative input is being suppressed by template-driven briefs. Run the **make-it-theirs play**: let them pitch freely, then reverse engineer SEO fit
- [ ] Find a shared pain point across 3+ internal teams. Build something simple (Google Sheet, Notion DB, dashboard) that solves it. **Do not call it an SEO project**
- [ ] Test the spectrum: am I *extracting* (asking favors), *being useful sometimes* (responding), or *building infrastructure* (SEO as a service)? Move toward the right end
- [ ] Stop assuming all internal teams understand what SEO does. Treat the first 6 months of a new role as a **credibility-building exercise**, not an optimization sprint
- [ ] For any cross-functional initiative, ask: *"Whose investment does this need to be a hit?"* Hand them the **starting point**, not the finished plan

### People to follow up

- **Bianca Anderson** — Growth Strategist, Stellar Search Signals · formerly Lead SEO at HubSpot, Organic Program Manager at Hims and Hers · [linkedin.com/in/bianca-anderson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bianca-anderson/) · DM for the HubSpot E-E-A-T Playbook chapter outline and the Hims constraints-first brief template.
- **Eli Schwartz** — for the 7 AEO media functions framework (referenced in the talk).
- **Erica Garza** — author, *Getting Off* · the staff writer in the make-it-theirs case study.
takeaways: SEOs only own 2 of 7 AEO functions per Eli Schwartz; 90% of citations come from third-party sources we don't control
Three plays: constraints first (treat blockers as collaborators), make it theirs (give up the starting point), SEO as a service (build shared infrastructure)
Constraints-first beat a years-blocked project at Hims: 50 pages, 7 figures of attributed revenue
Make-it-theirs: writer-led pitches out-ranked Reddit and converted 2× internal blog benchmarks
SEO as a service: build something that solves shared pain — but the pain has to be GENUINELY shared
Synthesis: constraints first builds credibility, make it theirs builds investment, SEO as a service builds dependency
Stop optimizing what you own; start influencing what you don't

## John Shehata — The Truth About Google Discover: 20 Pipelines, 100 Trillion Impressions, and the First-Ever Discover Core Update

**Key thesis:** Google Discover now drives **75% of Google traffic** for tracked publishers — up from 37% in 2023 — and CTR is **6× search**. Discover is not a different algorithm; it is search results sorted by personal interest and pushed to a feed. John mapped the full Discover pipeline (~20 sub-pipelines across ingestion, sorting, eligibility, assembly, and feedback) using NewzDash data on **100 trillion impressions and 55 million pages**. **February 2026 was Google's first-ever Discover-specific core update.** Winners: local stories, evergreen content, YouTube, X (with link cards), human-face images, longer headlines (12–15 words), em dashes (yes, really). Losers: listicles, international generalist publishers, sites with image quality below 1200px, sites pretending expertise outside their core topic.

![John Shehata on stage at SEO Week 2026 in his green Lacoste sweater + jeans, opening Day 3's Google Discover deep-dive](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fcm1922ed_IMG_2718%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

### TL;DR

Google Discover now drives 75% of Google traffic for tracked publishers, up from 37% in 2023, and CTR is 6× search. Discover is not a different algorithm. It is search results sorted by personal interest and pushed to a feed. John mapped the full Discover pipeline (~20 sub-pipelines across ingestion, sorting, eligibility, assembly, and feedback) using NewzDash data on 100 trillion impressions and 55 million pages. February 2026 was Google's first-ever Discover-specific core update. Winners: local, evergreen, YouTube, X with link cards, human-face images, 12–15 word headlines, em dashes. Losers: listicles, international generalists, sub-1200px images, sites sprawling outside their core topic.

### Why you should care about Discover

![Discover audience growth slide — 800M users (Google official, 2018) → ~1.2B today (NewzDash estimate, based on AI Overviews + 2B+ Android devices)](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fb111i709_IMG_2720%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

- Estimated **1.2 billion active users** globally (Google last disclosed 800M in 2018)
- For the publishers NewzDash tracks, Discover share of Google traffic grew from **37% in 2023 to 75% today**
- Search traffic share dropped to **25%** over the same period
- **Discover CTR is roughly 6× search CTR.** It is a feed, so users click and return repeatedly with no SERP distractions
- Discover is starting to roll out to **desktop**. John estimates desktop rollout will add **10–15% more traffic** for US publishers
- **Hard warning: do NOT get addicted.** Discover is volatile, unpredictable, and supplemental. Treating it as a strategy is like putting 75% of your portfolio in one stock
- **You cannot reliably measure Discover in GA4.** Best estimate: GA4 captures only ~10% of true Discover sessions. **Search Console is the only source of truth**

### The bridge to search you cannot ignore

- From a December 2025 Google webmaster meet slide (originally shared by a Google engineer): *"Continue to optimize your high-quality content for search to appear in Discover and avoid traffic volatility"*
- Reading bottom to top: **strong presence on search establishes your status as a trustworthy publisher, which then qualifies you for Discover**
- Most publishers who lose Discover traffic lose it because of a **search core update**, not a Discover-specific signal
- Until February 2026, that was always the mechanism. **February's update changed that.**

### Inside the Discover pipeline — 5 phases, ~20 sub-pipelines

![NewzDash "How Google Discover Works" pipeline diagram — 5 phases (Ingestion & Qualification → Sorting Hat with 150K clusters and 20 pipelines → Eligibility & Match with collection gates → Screen Assembly with ~150 concurrent A/B experiments and lane-specific freshness → Delivery & Feedback with NAJADES personalization). The full schematic referenced throughout this section.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2F90lb106f_IMG_2723%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

- **Phase 1 — Ingestion & Qualification.** Crawl, index, content extraction, entity recognition, broad eligibility check, image quality filter (under 1200px is heavily penalized), OG tags (`og:image`, `og:title`, `og:site_name` checked first, then falls back to title and H1)
- **Phase 2 — The Sorting Hat.** Topic classification using Google's unified taxonomy (Knowledge Graph, ~90 billion entities, same taxonomy used across Search, Trends, Ads). 150K clusters, 20 measured pipelines. Hard policy violations get filtered. AI summary tagging happens here — **29% of must-read content in AI Overviews in EN, near-zero in FR**
- **Phase 3 — Eligibility & Match.** Two questions: *is this story allowed to appear for this user* (collection gates), and *does this user actually want it?* Adult content, NSFW, misleading split images get blocked. Entity match between content and user interest profile decides what passes. **Binary kill switch** is an *asymmetric penalty* — suppression is wider than the corresponding boost
- **Phase 4 — Screen Assembly.** Google ranks the feed server-side (~150 concurrent A/B experiments per session), then re-ranks again on the device. Apple Intelligence may now apply additional personalization on top. **Freshness varies by lane:** 2.2–3.5 hours for breaking news, 2.5 days for shopping, 57 days for ads. Premium spots 2–4 = breaking news; deep spots 6+ = browse / shopping
- **Phase 5 — Delivery & Feedback Loop.** gRPC streaming + 24h background sync. Tracks dismissals, source blocks, follows, hearts, saves, engagement time. **Dismissed content creates permanent tombstones.** NAJADES personalization layer shapes the next refresh in real time

### The content-cluster types in Discover

![Discover content-cluster types diagram — 6 pipeline buckets connected to "Your Content" hub: Editorial Baseline (moonstone, aura, paginationpanoptic, relatedcontentruby), News & Urgency (mustntmiss, newsstoriesheadlines), Trends (deeptrendsfable, deeptrends), Local/Geo/Niche (geotargetingstories, webkicklocalstories, astria), Social & Video (creatorcontent, freshvideos 94% YouTube, neoncluster 100% YouTube), Commercial (shoppinginspiration, feedads 58.4% reach). Source: 1492.vision · 42M Discover cards · Dec 2025 – Feb 2026.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2F8nl4q2nv_IMG_2724%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

- **Editorial / Content cluster:** the largest bucket, most articles flow here (`moonstone`, `aura`, `paginationpanoptic`, `relatedcontentruby`)
- **Must Not Miss (`mustntmiss`):** exclusive content Google decides users should see, surfaced repeatedly across multiple days
- **News stories headlines (`newsstoriesheadlines`):** the same articles that appear when you type "news" in Search appear here
- **Trends (`deeptrendsfable`, `deeptrends`):** trend scanner from X.com + social media; trend-persistence layer
- **Local, Geo & Niche (`geotargetingstories`, `webkicklocalstories`, `astria`):** mainstream geo-filtered, hyperlocal/regional, vertical content
- **Social & Video (`creatorcontent`, `freshvideos`, `neoncluster`, `Discoverviewerrelatedcontent`, `userpersonascontent`):** **94% of `freshvideos` is YouTube; 100% of `neoncluster` is YouTube**
- **Commercial (`shoppinginspiration`, `feedads`):** **`feedads` reaches 58.4% of devices** with **a 57-day lookback window** for ad personalization

### Entities and headlines — the practical signal

- Entities = people, organizations, events, works of art, locations
- NewzDash analysis of 55M articles: **28% of all Discover articles include a person in the headline**
- People are the most common headline entity, followed by organizations, then locations
- Entity presence in headlines drives interest matching. If you write about a celebrity, **name the celebrity**. If you write about a city, **name the city**
- **OG tags are checked before page tags.** You can use a different OG title than your H1 to test what performs in Discover *without* changing your on-page SEO

### Performance varies dramatically by category

![GDdash "Performance by Category" heatmap — News dominates pages (28.36%), Pets & Animals tops CTR (8.65%), Hobbies & Leisure has longest persistence (6 days), Sensitive Subjects punches above weight (10% CTR). Columns: % Pages · % Impressions · % Clicks · % CTR · # days.](https://wsrv.nl/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcustomer-assets.emergentagent.com%2Fjob_github-checker-8%2Fartifacts%2Fzihp3wxs_IMG_2725%25202.jpg&w=1080&q=70&output=webp)

The performance-by-category heatmap is the single most actionable benchmark in the talk. **News** dominates pages (28%), but **Pets & Animals** has the highest CTR (8.65%) despite a 1.16% page share. **Hobbies & Leisure** holds the longest persistence at 6 days. **Law & Government** over-performs (6.48% pages → 15.29% clicks). **Sensitive Subjects** sits at 10% CTR — engagement is real but the lane is risky.

### February 2026 Discover core update — what changed

- Ran **February 5 to February 27, 2026**. **First-ever Discover-specific core update**
- Google's stated goals: more local content, more authoritative content (lift dates), better expertise evaluation
- **Shift from page-level authority to topic-level authority per site.** Publishers known for one topic get penalized for sprawling outside their lane
- Roughly **8% reduction in unique publishers** showing up in Discover post-update
- Local content surfaced more for local users. **International generalist publishers** (UK, US covering global stories) lost ground
- Multiple correction waves followed. NewzDash tracked **2–3 waves through mid-March** cleaning up over-corrections (sites that wrongly spiked to top 10 dropped back out)

### Format and surface winners and losers post-update

- **YouTube became the #1 surface in Discover after the update.** If you do not have a YouTube strategy, you are losing
- YouTube is dominated by news channels, so **legacy publishers benefit if they cross-publish**
- **X (Twitter) is now #2.** Critical X tactic: **post as a link card** (not as an image with link in body). With link cards, Discover routes the user directly to your article. With image posts, Discover routes through X first
- **Evergreen gained ~6 points of feed share. News articles dropped ~4 points**
- **Listicles got destroyed.** Visibility dropped from **~2% to ~0.6%**. Major format shift
- **First-person headlines still work.** Visibility climbed from **1.4% to 2.4%**. Example: *"67 years old, 2 weeks from retirement, and I got fired. Is this even legal?"* stayed in Discover for 3 months
- **Em dashes nearly doubled headline visibility.** Counter-intuitive given the AI-content concern, but the data is clear post-update
- **Click-bait and curiosity-gap headlines INCREASED post-update** in NewzDash analyses. Worth watching for further correction waves

### Headline length sweet spot

- **12–15 words is the optimal headline length** for Discover (excluding social posts which skew longer)
- **OG title is the lever.** You can test against your H1 *without affecting search rankings*
- Run continuous A/B tests on OG title length and entity placement

### Image guidance

- **Minimum 1200px width.** Below that triggers the low-quality-image filter and severely limits Discover eligibility
- **Human faces outperform every other image type.** Globes, illustrations, abstract images underperform
- **Avoid misleading split images** that imply a story not in the article. Triggers misleading-image filter

### The In-words / Out-words framework for content strategy

- **In-words:** topics that consistently work for your site in Discover. *Pull, target, repeat.* Example: a major US publisher discovered "recalls" content always performed in Discover. They now publish 2–3 recall stories weekly. Top traffic source for them
- **Riding the wave:** trending topics genuinely relevant to you. Standard play
- **Adjacent trend:** the most undervalued tactic. Identify what is trending elsewhere and find the connection to your topic
- *Architectural Digest example:* when Tom Cruise was trending around a *Mission Impossible* release, AD published *"where Tom Cruise hides when not on set: pictures from his house."* Worked **60–70% of the time**. They had house photography for nearly every celebrity, so any celebrity trend triggered the play

### Topic-level authority — a real change

- **John Mueller post-update:** a local site that proved expertise in gardening can now use that expertise as a topic credential
- Local sites *can* expand into adjacent topics if they demonstrate genuine expertise on each
- Generalist sites trying to play in every topic without depth got pushed down hardest
- **The signal:** build deep expertise, prove it, then expand carefully. **Don't sprawl.**

### The "safe search" diagnostic trick

- To check what % of your site Google considers NSFW: go to Google, run `site:yoursite.com` with `safe=active` appended to the URL
- Compare result count to your normal indexed pages. **The gap is content Google has flagged as not safe-search-eligible**
- If the % is meaningful (say 10%+), you may be losing Discover eligibility. **Move flagged content to a subdomain** to protect the main domain's Discover footprint

### Why publishers lose Discover traffic (per Google's official guidelines)

1. Changing reader interest in your topic over time
2. Content type mix shifting away from what got you in
3. Search core updates (still the #1 trigger historically)
4. Technical failures (especially OG tag breakage)
5. Content mismatch (headlines that don't deliver)
6. Seasonal demand (sports cycles, election cycles)
7. No social buzz or engagement signals
8. **Topical demotion at the category level.** Example: in late 2025, Google reportedly demoted **entertainment publishers from 100% baseline visibility to 20%**. The publishers did nothing wrong. The category itself was throttled

### Quotes worth keeping

> "Discover is now 75% of Google traffic for the publishers we track." — John Shehata

> "Discover is volatile and supplemental. It is not a strategy." — John Shehata

> "GA4 only captures about 10% of your real Discover sessions. Trust Search Console." — John Shehata

> "The key to remaining in Discover is to do well in search." — John Shehata

> "YouTube is now #1. X is #2. If you don't have a video and link-card strategy, you are losing." — John Shehata

> "In-words and out-words. Find what works. Repeat. Find what is adjacent. Capitalize." — John Shehata

### My take

This is the single most operational talk of Day 3 — and the one most publishers will need to re-watch in 90 days when the second correction wave from the February core update hits. John gave us **the schematic** for a system most SEOs treat as a black box.

The line that's going on the wall: **"Discover is volatile and supplemental. It is not a strategy."** Pair that with the 75% traffic-share stat and you have the central paradox of modern publishing — *the channel that drives the most traffic is also the most fragile, and the most likely to disappear with one update.* Plan the floor (search), enjoy the ceiling (Discover).

The **20-pipeline pipeline diagram** is the most useful single-slide reference I've seen at the conference. The mental model goes from *"Discover = ranking magic"* to *"Discover = a sortable feed pipeline with discrete signals at each stage that I can audit."* Every publisher should print this and tape it to the SEO team's wall.

**Three of John's findings should be in everyone's editorial brief by Monday:**

1. **OG title is the Discover lever, not H1.** Test 12–15 word OG titles with named entities against your existing H1. Search ranking is unaffected. Discover impressions move materially.
2. **YouTube is now the #1 surface.** Garrett Sussman's morning talk on personalization data already pointed at this. John's pipeline data confirms it: `freshvideos` is 94% YouTube, `neoncluster` is 100% YouTube. **If you don't ship video, you don't ship Discover.**
3. **In-words framework.** Run a 90-day backfill in Search Console: which topics deliver Discover impressions repeatedly? Build the editorial calendar around those, not around your competitor's keyword set.

Pair this with Ross Simmonds's *"create once, distribute forever"* and Bianca Anderson's *"influence the other 5 functions"* and you have the operating model: **build a topic moat → distribute it across YouTube + X (link cards) + Discover-eligible templates → measure in Search Console → don't get addicted.** The first-person-headline finding is the same E-E-A-T point Andrea Volpini made on Day 1, in different language. **Every layer of John's data agrees with itself.**

### Open questions

- [ ] Will the click-bait / curiosity-gap rebound be a permanent shift, or is another correction wave coming?
- [ ] How does Apple Intelligence's new on-device personalization layer interact with Google's server-side ranking (NAJADES)?
- [ ] What is the right cadence to A/B test OG title variations against H1 without losing tracking continuity?
- [ ] For non-news sites, what is the equivalent of the "in-words" framework? How do B2B SaaS or e-commerce brands find their *recall*-equivalent topic?
- [ ] How does Discover desktop rollout affect publishers whose audience skews mobile?
- [ ] Will the topic-authority shift from February 2026 propagate back to search core updates later this year?

### Action items

- [ ] **Pull Discover impressions from Search Console** (not GA4) for the last 90 days. Track separately from search traffic
- [ ] **Audit OG image dimensions** across the site. Anything under 1200px wide gets flagged for replacement
- [ ] Audit OG titles. Test **12–15 word variants** against H1 for top Discover-eligible templates
- [ ] Audit headlines for entity inclusion. Add named people, organizations, locations where appropriate
- [ ] **Identify in-words:** which topics consistently produce Discover traffic for your site? Build an editorial calendar that publishes these on a recurring schedule
- [ ] **Identify adjacent trends:** what is trending in your industry that you can credibly tie to your existing content moat?
- [ ] **Run the `safe=active` diagnostic.** Calculate your NSFW-flagged page percentage. Migrate flagged content to a subdomain if material
- [ ] **Build a YouTube content strategy.** Cross-publish key articles as video. Optimize for Discover's video cluster
- [ ] **Switch X posting to link cards** (not image-with-link). Audit recent posts and republish in card format if traffic loss is suspected
- [ ] **Stop publishing listicles for Discover.** Reallocate that production capacity to first-person, evergreen, or video
- [ ] Audit the breadth of topics on the site. Identify your strongest topic moat. **Pull back from sprawling outside it** unless you can prove genuine expertise
- [ ] Subscribe to **NewzDash** for ongoing Discover tracking and the upcoming GoogleX virtual conference
- [ ] Watch the second-wave correction window for the February core update. Expect adjustment volatility through Q2
